name: Meedan Check
purpose: Collaborative platform for fact-checking desks: ingests claims from tiplines and social monitoring, deduplicates against previously checked items, assigns and tracks verification tasks across a team, and publishes outputs.
journalism_use_case: The operational backbone for a tipline-driven desk: a WhatsApp tipline feeds Check, incoming claims are matched against work already done, and the remaining novel claims are assigned to reporters with an auditable status trail — the difference between a desk that scales and one that re-verifies the same rumour weekly.
pros: Purpose-built for fact-checking desk workflow rather than adapted from generic ticketing — tipline ingestion, claim deduplication and publication are first-class
Self-hostable under MIT, so claims and reader submissions can stay on infrastructure you control
Used by fact-checking organisations in multiple countries and sustained by an established non-profit, giving it institutional durability
Pairs with Alegre for similarity matching, so the deduplication is real rather than keyword-based
cons: Multi-service stack (Docker, PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Redis) with non-trivial operational burden; the public dev-environment repository is not a production install, which trips teams up
Similarity matching produces ranked probabilistic suggestions, not determinations that two claims are the same — a reviewer must adjudicate
Optional integrations send data off-box: Google Translate API, Sentry error reporting, Smooch/Sunshine Conversations for messaging — each needs a deliberate decision
Release cadence is modest (v0.194.0, 2026-02-10 with last push 2026-09-23), and 131 stars means a thin external community for self-hosters
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: Meedan publishes Check as the platform behind partner tiplines, and the repository shows sustained multi-year development with 131 stars and only 7 open issues. The 'dev environment, not production install' caveat is stated by the project itself.
assessment: The right choice if you are running a claims desk with reader submissions; overkill if you are not. For your profile the honest read is that self-hosting Check is a platform-engineering commitment comparable to OpenAleph, so I would only recommend it where tipline volume justifies it. Disable the Google Translate and Sentry integrations by default — a translation call on a reader's submitted message is a disclosure of that reader's material to a third party.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-23, latest release v0.194.0 (2026-02-10), 131 stars, 7 open issues. Low open-issue count and a long release history under an established non-profit; the two-month gap since last push is normal for a platform at this stage. Classified active on institutional backing plus release history, not push recency.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the platform; bundled ML components live in Alegre and carry their own terms.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a multi-container deployment with PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Redis — realistically one well-provisioned VM minimum, more for tipline volume. Optional paid dependencies if you enable Google Translate or a messaging provider (not priced here). Operating effort is the dominant cost.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps claims and submitted media on your infrastructure, which matters because tipline content can identify the person who submitted it. The optional integrations are the exposure points and should be off by default. Reader-submitted material deserves the same handling discipline as source material.
alternatives: Alegre alone if you only need similarity matching inside an existing workflow
ClaimsKG extractor or the Google Fact Check Tools API for checking whether a claim is already debunked
A simple issue tracker plus Alegre for a small desk that cannot operate the full stack

name: Alegre (Meedan)
purpose: Multilingual and multimodal similarity service exposing text, image, audio and video similarity search over a vector index, used as the matching engine behind Meedan Check.
journalism_use_case: Powers tipline and fact-check deduplication at scale: when a reader submits an image or claim, Alegre finds whether a near-identical item has already been received and checked, so the desk answers from existing work instead of re-verifying. At high tipline volume this is the difference between a functioning service and a backlog.
pros: Multimodal in one service — text, image, audio and video similarity — which is otherwise four separate integrations
Self-hostable, so media and hashes stay on infrastructure you control; important because tipline media is often sensitive
MIT licensed with an active tag cadence (v0.187.2) and real production use behind Check
Solves a specific, measurable problem (duplicate workload) rather than promising verification
cons: Similarity answers 'have we seen this before?', not 'is this real?' — it provides no synthetic-media or manipulation detection, and conflating the two is a serious misreading
Bundles third-party sentence-transformer and BERT checkpoints whose own licences were not verified in this survey — a real gap for commercial redistribution
Requires Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, PostgreSQL and Docker; optional Google Translate integration sends text off-box
Tiny external community (15 stars, 22 open issues) and no GitHub release objects — effectively a Meedan internal service published openly, so self-hosting support is limited
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Production evidence is structural: Alegre is the matching layer of Meedan Check, which is deployed by fact-checking partners. The unverified bundled-model licences are an explicit gap carried into this entry rather than resolved.
assessment: Worth running only as part of a Check deployment or where you specifically need multimodal near-duplicate matching at volume. For your profile a lighter alternative — ImageHash plus a sentence-transformers index — gives you most of the capability with components you control and whose licences you can verify. Alegre's advantage is that it is already integrated and battle-tested; its disadvantage is opacity about the models inside it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-28, latest tag v0.187.2, no GitHub release objects, 15 stars, 22 open issues. Continuous versioned tagging driven by Check's needs; maintenance is institutional rather than community-driven.
model_or_data_licence: Varies — bundles third-party sentence-transformer/BERT checkpoints whose own licences were NOT verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted; unresolved uncertainty at the bundled-model layer. Verify the specific checkpoints before commercial redistribution.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch plus PostgreSQL plus model-serving containers; GPU helpful for embedding throughput. Optional Google Translate API charges if enabled (not priced here). Estimate.
privacy: Self-hostable so media and hashes remain yours. Optional translation and LLM integrations send text to third parties if configured — review before enabling, since tipline text can identify a submitter.
alternatives: ImageHash plus sentence-transformers for a self-assembled, licence-verifiable equivalent
ThreatExchange PDQ/vPDQ for standards-based perceptual hashing of images and video
Meedan Check, which bundles Alegre and is the usual reason to run it

name: Fetch (Meedan ClaimReview aggregator)
purpose: Service that pulls fact-check outputs from heterogeneous publisher feeds and normalises them into ClaimReview-structured records for indexing.
journalism_use_case: Reference implementation for normalising fact-check feeds so a newsroom can query across many fact-checking organisations' outputs from one index — in principle letting a desk check 'has anyone already debunked this?' without visiting a dozen sites.
pros: Addresses a genuine interoperability gap: fact-check publication formats are inconsistent and ClaimReview normalisation is the accepted fix
MIT licensed with the ClaimReview mapping patterns readable in source — useful as documentation even if you do not run it
Authored by an organisation deeply involved in fact-check interoperability standards
cons: ARCHIVED — GitHub API confirms archived=true, last push 2026-05-21. It is read-only and will receive no fixes
Feed adapters for third-party sites rot quickly by nature; an archived adapter collection is close to worthless operationally
Essentially no community (1 star, 9 open issues at archival)
Fetches from third-party fact-checker sites, so your crawling pattern is visible to them
feedback: No individual user reports. The decisive documented fact is the archival status, confirmed by the GitHub API on 2026-11-17 (archived=true). That makes all other assessment secondary.
assessment: Reference only. Read it to understand ClaimReview normalisation patterns, then use the Google Fact Check Tools API or ClaimsKG for the actual lookup. For your profile the lesson generalises: feed-adapter collections are the most perishable category of software in this catalogue, and depending on an unmaintained one means silent coverage loss rather than visible failure.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2026-05-21, latest tag v0.184.9, 1 star, 9 open issues. Archived by the maintainer — the strongest possible maintenance signal, and unambiguous.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is frozen.
privacy: Fetches from third-party fact-checker sites and APIs; your crawling traffic is visible to them. No credentials required for most sources.
alternatives: Google Fact Check Tools API for claim lookup (hosted, Google terms)
ClaimsKG extractor for building your own cross-organisation fact-check database — but note its own licence is unconfirmed
Meedan Check, which supersedes this component operationally
blockers: Archived by the maintainer — do not build on it

name: InVID-WeVerify Verification Plugin
purpose: Browser extension aggregating verification tools: video keyframe extraction, reverse image search across multiple engines, EXIF inspection, magnifier and forensic filters, deepfake and synthetic-media detection panels, archiving and OCR.
journalism_use_case: Front-line triage of a viral image or video claim: establish whether media is recycled, find the earliest appearance, inspect metadata, and gather forensic signals before publishing a verification. It is the single most widely used verification tool among working journalists, because it puts a dozen techniques one click away.
pros: Breadth and accessibility: a reporter with no technical background can run keyframe extraction plus multi-engine reverse search in under a minute, which is why it dominates practical newsroom verification
Actively maintained with a current release (v0.94, 2026-11-03) and pushed 2026-11-17, backed by AFP and an EU research consortium rather than a volunteer
Extension code is MIT, so the client side is auditable
Consolidates workflows (keyframes, reverse search, EXIF, archiving) that would otherwise require four separate tools and manual file shuffling
cons: NOT local-only, and this is the critical caveat: media submitted for keyframes, forensics, deepfake detection, translation or archiving is uploaded to AFP/vera.ai backend services, and reverse search sends it to Google, Baidu and Yandex. Submitting unpublished source material is a disclosure

Forensic and deepfake panel outputs are probabilistic signals and investigative leads, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation or synthesis — false positives and negatives occur, and platform recompression degrades every forensic signal
Matomo analytics is present in the extension, so usage telemetry exists
Backend model weights are not distributed and their licences were not verified, so you cannot reproduce or audit the detector outputs
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey, but the plugin's standing among verification practitioners is well documented by the InVID/WeVerify/vera.ai projects and by its adoption in verification training curricula. The upload-to-backend behaviour and the Matomo analytics are documented in the project's own privacy information — treat these as project-disclosed facts, not inferences.
assessment: Adopt it for public, already-circulating media — that is the case it is built for and it is excellent there. Write an explicit rule against using it on unpublished source material, because the convenient buttons are the ones that upload. For media-in-exile work, note additionally that reverse-image search through Yandex or Baidu discloses the image to jurisdictions you may be investigating. Treat every forensic panel as a lead that must be corroborated by non-forensic reporting.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v0.94 (2026-11-03), 53 stars, 28 open issues. Same-day push with a current release; funded consortium backing (AFP Medialab, vera.ai). Star count understates adoption because users install from browser stores, not GitHub.
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the extension; deepfake and forensics models run on AFP/vera.ai backend services, weights not distributed and model licences not verified.
licence_restrictions: Extension code unrestricted. The backend services operate under the consortium's terms, not an open licence, so the analytical capability is not self-hostable.
costs: Free to use. No infrastructure. The cost is non-monetary: dependency on third-party backends you do not control and cannot audit.
privacy: The weakest privacy profile among widely recommended verification tools, and it must be understood plainly: media sent to the forensics, deepfake, keyframe, translation or archiving panels is uploaded to AFP/vera.ai; reverse-image search sends the image to Google, Baidu and Yandex; Matomo analytics records usage. Appropriate for public media, inappropriate for unpublished source material.
alternatives: Sherloq for a fully local image-forensics workbench
PySceneDetect plus ExifTool plus ImageHash for a local equivalent of the keyframe and metadata workflow
Hosted verification services only where the media is already public
blockers: Uploads media to third-party backends — unsuitable for unpublished or source-sensitive material

name: ClaimBuster-Spotter
purpose: Transformer-based model that scores sentences for check-worthiness — how much a statement looks like a factual claim a fact-checker would want to verify.
journalism_use_case: Automatically rank sentences from debate transcripts, speeches or long interviews by check-worthiness so a fact-checking desk can prioritise which statements to verify under deadline — triage, when a two-hour speech produces 800 sentences and the desk has three hours.
pros: Addresses a real deadline problem — prioritisation, not adjudication — and is honest about being a ranking signal
Can run locally with no third-party calls for the models in this repository, unlike the hosted claimbuster.org API
GPL-3.0 code with published research behind the approach, so the method is citable in a methodology note
cons: Dormant: last push 2023-11-29, no releases or tags, 87 stars with 26 open issues — a research artefact that has stopped moving
Check-worthiness scores are probabilistic prioritisation signals, not judgements of truth: a high score means 'worth checking', not 'false', and this is routinely misread
Trained predominantly on US political discourse, so transfer to other political cultures and languages is unevidenced
Trained checkpoints are not clearly licensed in-repo, and the hosted ClaimBuster API has separate terms — using the hosted API sends your text to the university's service
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the dormancy (no push since November 2023), the GPL-3.0 code licence, and the unclear checkpoint licensing. The ClaimBuster project itself is well cited in the automated-fact-checking literature, which is research credibility rather than deployment evidence.
assessment: Not something I would deploy in 2026: dormant, US-centric, and the capability can be reproduced with a modern instruction-tuned model and a clear prompt, with better multilingual coverage. Its catalogue value is conceptual — check-worthiness as a distinct, modest, well-scoped task is the right way to apply automation to fact-checking, as opposed to asking a model for verdicts. Keep as reference.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2023-11-29, no releases, no tags, 87 stars, 26 open issues. Three years without activity and an open backlog; no deprecation notice. Dormant rather than archived.
model_or_data_licence: NOT verified — trained checkpoints are not clearly licensed in-repo; the hosted ClaimBuster API has its own terms.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on code limits embedding in proprietary newsroom tooling. Checkpoint licensing is unresolved, so redistribution of trained weights is legally unclear.
costs: No fee. TensorFlow-era dependencies make the install awkward; CPU or modest GPU sufficient. ClaimBuster datasets requested separately.
privacy: Runs locally with no third-party calls for the in-repo models. Using claimbuster.org's hosted API instead sends your text to that service — avoid for unpublished material.
alternatives: A self-hosted instruction-tuned LLM with an explicit check-worthiness prompt, which covers more languages
Loki or FacTool for claim extraction — but note both default to hosted LLM APIs
Manual triage by an editor, which remains competitive for a single speech

name: FEVER platform and baselines
purpose: Benchmark dataset, annotation platform and baseline systems for fact extraction and verification: given a claim, retrieve evidence sentences from Wikipedia and classify as supported, refuted or not-enough-info.
journalism_use_case: Standard reference point for evaluating any evidence-retrieval-plus-entailment pipeline before trusting it on real claims. The annotation platform is independently reusable for building a newsroom's own claim/evidence gold set — which is the only honest way to know whether a tool works on your material.
pros: The reusable annotation platform is the underrated asset: it lets you construct your own labelled claim/evidence set rather than extrapolating from published benchmarks
Fully local once the data is downloaded, with no API keys required — unusual among fact-verification tooling
Apache-2.0 code and a widely cited benchmark, so results are comparable to the published literature
Establishes the discipline of measuring retrieval and entailment separately, which is diagnostically useful
cons: Claims are human-written over Wikipedia, not real-world political or social-media claims, so FEVER scores systematically overstate real-world performance — the single most important caveat when a vendor cites a FEVER number
Baseline checkpoints are downloaded separately and their licences were not verified; the Wikipedia evidence corpus is CC-BY-SA, which carries ShareAlike obligations on derived corpora
Low activity: pushed 2026-02-20, no releases or tags, 130 stars — a benchmark artefact rather than a maintained product
Verdicts are probabilistic classifications, never proof, and the three-way label scheme does not match editorial reality
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: FEVER is among the most cited benchmarks in automated fact verification; its Wikipedia-derived construction and the resulting optimism bias are discussed in the subsequent literature (including AVeriTeC's framing of why a more realistic benchmark was needed).
assessment: Useful to you as a measuring instrument and an annotation tool, not as a capability. Concretely: when someone proposes an AI fact-checking tool, ask what it scores on real claims rather than FEVER, and use the annotation platform to build a small gold set from your own published fact-checks to test it. That is a higher-value use of FEVER than running its baselines.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-20, no releases or tags, 130 stars, 1 open issue. Benchmark artefacts are expected to be static once published; the near-empty issue tracker is consistent with a finished research release rather than neglect.
model_or_data_licence: NOT verified — baseline checkpoints are downloaded separately. The Wikipedia evidence corpus is CC-BY-SA.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. CC-BY-SA on the Wikipedia evidence corpus imposes attribution and ShareAlike obligations if you redistribute a derived evidence corpus.
costs: No fee. Requires substantial local disk for the Wikipedia dump and dataset, plus a Python ML stack. No paid APIs. Estimate.
privacy: Fully local once data is downloaded; no third-party API keys required. Suitable for use on an isolated machine.
alternatives: AVeriTeC for a benchmark closer to real fact-checking practice — but its licence is unconfirmed
X-FACT for multilingual claim classification evaluation
Building your own gold set from your newsroom's published fact-checks, using FEVER's annotation platform

name: AVeriTeC dataset and baseline
purpose: Benchmark of real-world claims checked by fact-checking organisations, modelling verification as question generation, question answering over open web evidence, and the production of a written justification.
journalism_use_case: The closest public benchmark to actual fact-checking practice: it models verification the way a fact-checker works — asking sub-questions, finding evidence for each, then writing a justification — so it is the right yardstick for judging whether an AI assistant could plausibly support a desk.
pros: Built from real claims already checked by fact-checking organisations, so performance figures mean substantially more than FEVER's Wikipedia-derived scores
The question-answer-justify decomposition matches editorial method and makes model output auditable step by step rather than as a bare label
Includes a written-justification requirement, which exposes models that get the label right for the wrong reasons
cons: Licence could NOT be confirmed: no LICENSE or COPYING file in the repository root, GitHub API reports no detected licence, and the README has no licence section — redistribution and commercial terms are unknown and this is unresolved
Requires a Google Programmable Search API key and CSE ID for coarse retrieval, so claim text and generated queries are sent to Google's Search API — not a local pipeline
Dormant: last push 2024-11-27, no releases, 84 stars
Verdicts are probabilistic model outputs requiring human adjudication, and the benchmark's own task remains far from solved
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented finding is the licence gap, verified in session 1 by checking for LICENSE/COPYING and the GitHub licence API, and retained here as unresolved. The benchmark is well cited in the automated-fact-checking literature.
assessment: Valuable intellectually, unusable as infrastructure. For your profile the right use is to borrow its evaluation design — decompose a claim into sub-questions, require an evidence trail and a written justification — when assessing any AI tool a vendor pitches to your newsroom. Do not redistribute the dataset or build a product on it until the licence position is clarified with the authors.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-11-27, no releases, no tags, no detected licence, 84 stars, 4 open issues. Two years without activity; typical academic release-and-move-on pattern.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — no LICENSE/COPYING file in the repository root, GitHub licence API reports none, README has no licence section
model_or_data_licence: n/a — no weights distributed. Dataset terms also unconfirmed.
licence_restrictions: Unresolved. Treat redistribution and commercial use as legally unclear until clarified with the authors. Note that the underlying claims come from fact-checking organisations whose own content terms may also apply.
costs: No software fee. Requires a Google Programmable Search API key (paid above the free quota — current rates not verified here) and large local disk, plus an LLM for question generation (cost depends on provider). Estimate.
privacy: NOT local: claim text and generated queries are sent to Google's Search API, and depending on model choice to an LLM provider. Retrieved pages are cached locally. Unsuitable for unpublished claims about sensitive subjects.
alternatives: FEVER where a clearly licensed benchmark is required
X-FACT for multilingual evaluation under an MIT licence
Full Fact AI Trust Benchmark for a practitioner-authored evaluation of assistant tools
blockers: No licence file — redistribution and commercial use legally unresolved
Requires Google Search API; not a local pipeline

name: X-FACT
purpose: Multilingual benchmark of claims and fact-check verdicts drawn from fact-checking sites in 25 languages, with harmonised labels for evaluating cross-lingual claim classification.
journalism_use_case: Lets a newsroom test whether an automated claim-classification or claim-matching approach actually transfers to the languages it publishes in, rather than assuming English-trained performance carries over — a directly relevant question for any outlet publishing in several languages or in exile.
pros: Multilingual coverage (25 languages) is the specific gap it fills; almost every other benchmark here is English-only
MIT licensed, which — unusually among these academic datasets — makes reuse legally clear
Fully local with no API keys required, so evaluation can run on an isolated machine
cons: A benchmark, not a tool: it classifies claims against labels from fact-checking sites without retrieving evidence, so models trained on it learn surface and metadata cues as much as factuality — a known shortcut problem
Labels harmonised across organisations with different verdict scales, which introduces mapping noise that limits how precisely results can be interpreted
Dormant: last push 2024-10-04, no releases, 31 stars — minimal community
No weights distributed, so you must bring your own multilingual model
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: MIT licence confirmed via the GitHub API; 31 stars and no activity since October 2024. Cited in the multilingual fact-checking literature.
assessment: Narrow but legitimately useful to you for one specific decision: before trusting any claim-matching component across your publication languages, measure it here. Treat the absolute numbers sceptically because of the evidence-free task design, but the relative drop between English and your other languages is the informative signal — and that drop is usually large. Keep as a reference instrument.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-10-04, no releases or tags, 31 stars, 1 open issue. Over two years inactive; static dataset artefact, which limits the practical harm of dormancy.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — no weights distributed. Note the underlying claims derive from fact-checking sites whose own content terms may apply to redistribution.
licence_restrictions: Code and dataset packaging are MIT. Upstream publisher content rights are a residual consideration if you republish claim text.
costs: No fee. Python ML stack plus whichever multilingual model you evaluate; GPU helpful. No paid APIs.
alternatives: AVeriTeC for a more realistic task design — but licence unconfirmed
FEVER for English evidence-retrieval evaluation
Building a gold set from your own newsroom's multilingual fact-checks

name: ClaimsKG extractor
purpose: Scraper and knowledge-graph builder that extracts published fact-checks from fact-checking websites and emits a structured RDF knowledge graph of claims, verdicts and entities.
journalism_use_case: Build a cross-organisation database of already-published fact-checks (Full Fact, Snopes, PolitiFact, Africa Check, AFP Fact Check, EUvsDisinfo) so a desk can check whether a circulating claim has already been debunked before spending reporter time on it.
pros: Produces a structured, queryable knowledge graph rather than a flat list, so you can ask cross-cutting questions (which claims about a given entity have been checked, by whom, with what verdict)
Covers a useful spread of fact-checking organisations including non-Western ones (Africa Check), which the Google Fact Check API under-represents
Self-hosted scraping means you are not dependent on a vendor API's quota or deprecation
cons: Licence could NOT be confirmed: the GitHub licence API returns 404 and no LICENSE file is detected; the code is also a fork of vwoloszyn/fake_news_extractor, which compounds provenance uncertainty — reuse is legally unresolved
Dormant: last push 2022-09-01, tag v0.2, 21 stars, 0 open issues — four years inactive, and web scrapers decay faster than almost any other code because target sites change
Scrapes third-party fact-checker websites directly, so your crawling traffic is visible to them and may breach their terms
English-dominant coverage despite the multi-organisation ambition
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the licence gap (GitHub licence API 404, no LICENSE file) and the fork provenance, both recorded in session 1 and retained; last push 2022-09-01.
assessment: Not usable as-is: a four-year-old scraper against sites that have certainly changed, with no licence. The idea is sound and worth reimplementing if cross-organisation fact-check lookup matters to you — but build it against ClaimReview markup (which publishers emit deliberately) rather than by scraping, and consider the Google Fact Check Tools API for coverage with the trade-off that queries go to Google.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2022-09-01, latest tag v0.2, no releases, no detected licence, 21 stars, 0 open issues. Four years inactive. For a web scraper this is effectively non-functional, since target site structures will have changed.
licence: NOT CONFIRMED — GitHub licence API returns 404 and no LICENSE file detected; code is a fork of vwoloszyn/fake_news_extractor, compounding provenance uncertainty
licence_restrictions: Unresolved. Do not redistribute or build a product on it. Separately, scraping fact-checkers' sites may breach their terms of use regardless of the code licence.
costs: No fee. Operating cost would be scraper maintenance, which is the dominant and recurring cost of this approach.
privacy: Scrapes third-party fact-checker websites directly; your crawling pattern and IP are visible to those sites. No credentials required.
alternatives: Google Fact Check Tools API for maintained claim lookup (hosted, Google terms, ClaimReview-based coverage)
Writing your own ClaimReview harvester against publishers' structured markup
Meedan Check if you need a desk workflow rather than a lookup database
blockers: No licence file and fork provenance unclear — legally unresolved
Four-year-old scraper against changed target sites

name: Loki (OpenFactVerification)
purpose: Pipeline that decomposes a text into discrete checkable claims, retrieves evidence via a search API, and uses an LLM to produce per-claim verdicts with cited sources.
journalism_use_case: First-pass screening of a long text — a press release, transcript, filed story or AI-generated draft — into a ranked list of discrete checkable claims with candidate evidence links, which a journalist then verifies manually.
pros: Claim decomposition is the genuinely useful part: turning prose into an enumerated list of atomic factual assertions is tedious human work and the model does it adequately
MIT licensed with a clear pipeline structure, so the decomposition stage can be reused independently of the verdict stage
Produces cited evidence links rather than bare verdicts, which at least makes the output checkable
cons: NOT local: an OPENAI_API_KEY is required for all tasks per the README, and a SERPER_API_KEY for evidence retrieval — submitted text and generated queries go to OpenAI and a Google Search proxy. Unsuitable for unpublished material

Verdicts are LLM-generated probabilistic assessments with known failure modes — hallucinated reasoning, over-trust in low-quality retrieved sources, sensitivity to prompt and search ranking — so they are assistance, not adjudication
Dormant: last push 2024-10-03, latest release v0.0.2 (2024-04-21), 1,165 stars with only 3 open issues — the low issue count here reflects abandonment rather than triage
Hard-wired to specific providers, so swapping in a self-hosted model is a code change rather than configuration
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the mandatory OpenAI and Serper API keys stated in the project's README; dormancy since October 2024; 1,165 stars indicating initial interest that did not convert into sustained maintenance.
assessment: Avoid for new deployment as an end-to-end tool: it is dormant and its architecture sends your text to third parties by design. If claim decomposition is what you want, reimplement that one stage against a self-hosted model — it is a modest prompt-engineering task and keeps the material inside the perimeter. The broader judgement for your work: LLM verdict generation on public-interest claims is the wrong shape of automation, because the expensive part of fact-checking is evidence judgement, which is exactly what the model does worst.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-10-03, latest release v0.0.2 (2024-04-21), 1,165 stars, 3 open issues. Over two years inactive. The very low open-issue count against high stars indicates the tracker is unattended rather than well managed.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — calls hosted LLM APIs rather than bundling weights; those providers' terms govern use.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. The binding constraints are the third-party API terms you must accept to run it at all.
costs: Software free, but operation requires paid APIs: an OpenAI key (token charges — current rates not verified here) and a Serper search key (paid above free tier — not verified here). Running it over a long document is a real per-use cost, not an estimate of infrastructure.
privacy: NOT local. Submitted text, extracted claims and generated queries are sent to OpenAI and Serper. Unsuitable for unpublished material, source documents, or anything whose subject should not learn it is being checked.
alternatives: FacTool for a similar architecture — but it shares the hosted-API dependency and is also dormant
A self-hosted LLM performing claim decomposition only, with human evidence judgement
DEFAME for multimodal claims with an auditable tool-by-tool evidence trail — also hosted-LLM dependent by default
blockers: Requires OpenAI and Serper API keys — text leaves your infrastructure by design
